evidence:
Workbook row 2: 'Keeps an authentic human voice (casual/terse is good); not robotic, over-polished, or LLM-generated prose.' Skill quality-checks.md check 2: verify 'sentence variety, contractions, the occasional terse fragment in the notes'; defect is 'uniform cadence, marketing gloss, perfectly parallel bullets, or a voice that changes between instruction.md and the notes'.

What holds up. task/instruction.md (5 lines, 116 words) is first person and specific to one person's habit: line 1 'I'd like a small local playground ... I often paste a long one-line experiment, format it, make changes in several places, and then run it beside the source.' Sentence lengths vary (a 7-word 'The editor itself matters' clause against a 23-word habit sentence), there is a contraction, no bullets, no headings, no numbered list. A grep of instruction.md and all six notes for seamless|robust|delve|leverage|comprehensive|intuitive|ensure|utilize|streamline|powerful and for em/en dashes returned zero hits. No note uses a bullet list, so there are no parallel bullets. The first-person speaker carries into the notes: overview.md:3 'while I work'; behaviour.md:11 'That refresh must not touch what I'm doing ... say so and keep my draft; do not load the newer revision over my work'; ui.md:3 'the source I see', ui.md:9 'for as long as I keep typing at those carets, however slowly', ui.md:3 'Don't use a textarea'. Terse fragments exist in the notes: security.md:5 'Save source as text.', ui.md:11 'Navigation wraps at the ends.', ui.md:15 'A standalone formatter is allowed.' British spelling (behaviour, colour) is consistent across the notes.

Bounded voice observations (not judged a defect, recorded for the owner):
(a) policy.md:5 'Use the public behaviour in these notes as the contract. The examples are ways to explain it, not exact selectors, CSS classes or implementation requirements.' This is authoring/review vocabulary rather than the speaker of instruction.md; a person asking for a playground does not call their own notes 'public behaviour' or disclaim 'exact selectors'. It is the one place the register clearly breaks.
(b) integration.md:1,3 switch to plural 'How we start the app' / 'We start it with node /app/server.js' while every other file that has a speaker uses 'I'. The frozen template integration.md is impersonal ('The application runs as one Node 22 process'), so the 'we' is task-authored.
(c) behaviour.md is the most specification-like note: 10 'must'/'must not' in 514 words and stacked compound sentences such as behaviour.md:9 'One tab's later successful Save must make the other's old-revision Save fail without changing the saved record or discarding that tab's dirty draft.' and the 62-word sentence at behaviour.md:3 beginning 'Errors go to that same console:'. The notes total 19 'must'/'must not' against none in instruction.md. The register is denser and more normative than the brief, though the same first-person speaker is still present in that file.
(d) The stiff phrase 'describes the starting scope' appears in both instruction.md:3 and integration.md:7.

Why Note and not Fail: none of the skill's named defects is present in full. There is no marketing gloss, no bullet structure, no uniform cadence, and the speaker identity (first person, same concerns) is continuous from the brief into overview, behaviour and ui. The shift in (c) is a shift in density inside detail notes, which the skill expects to carry detail, and (a)/(b) are two isolated sentences. No runtime or judge evidence applies to this row; the verdict rests on reading the frozen text only.
suggested_fix: Optional, wording only: rewrite policy.md:5 in the speaker's voice (e.g. 'What these notes describe is what I care about; where I give an example it is only to explain, not a required class name or layout.'), change integration.md 'we' to 'I' or to the impersonal form, and replace 'describes the starting scope' with plainer words. Any such edit changes the task bytes and invalidates this clearance.
